title: Benford’s Law Anomaly Detector
text:
Benford’s Law is often seen as the go-to forensic accounting tool in fraud detection.
📈 I built this interactive Shiny app to let users:

Upload their own .csv files (max. 500MB) [note: please be patient, upload time is slow…]
Select a numeric column to analyse
Automatically extract the first digits
Compare the digit distribution to Benford’s expected probabilities
Flag anomalies using a \(\chi^2\) (Chi-squared) test (checks whether the difference between predicted results and actual values is statistically significant)

Here is the Benford’s Law Anomaly Detector I made.
Click the link above to launch the live app hosted on shinyapps.io.


🔍What is Benford’s Law?
Although Simon Newcomb first noted the mathematical property, today’s widely known Benford’s Law is a curious statistical principle used in anomaly detection. It reveals that in many real-world datasets, small leading digits (i.e. 1) are counter-intuitively more likely to occur than large digits. This pattern seems to be present in a wide range of cases, ranging from:

🗳 election results;
🏡 street addresses;
📊 financial data;
⚰️ mortality statistics;
🧪 to molecular weights.







📐 Generalised Benford’s Law: The Formula Behind the Pattern


The probability that a number begins with digit d (from 1 through 9) is:


\[P(d) = \log_{10} \left(1 + \frac{1}{d} \right)\]


Where:



\(P(d)\) is the probability that the first digit is \(d\)
The logarithm is base-10
This formula shows why 1 appears about 30.1% of the time, while 9 only shows up around 4.6%






📊 Benford’s Law Expected Distribution
The plot below shows the probability distribution predicted by Benford’s Law for the first digit (1–9). As you can see, the digit 1 appears ~30% of the time, while 9 appears less than 5%.

title: CGT Calculator
text:
What is Capital Gains Tax (CGT)?
CGT is levied on profit derived from the disposal of a CGT asset acquired on or after 20 September 1985, where the realisation is not undertaken in the ordinary course of carrying on a business; otherwise, the gain will be assessable under s6-5.
According to s108-5(2), CGT assets encompass: land and buildings (including rental properties), shares in a company, units in a unit trust, rights and options, leases, goodwill, debts owed to a taxpayer, foreign currency, and cryptocurrencies (such as Bitcoin).
The net capital gain derived from the disposal of a CGT asset is considered as statutory income and is included in the taxpayer’s income tax return under Item 18 (s105-5).
However, if an overall net capital loss arises, the amount is not deductible in the income year it occurred. Instead, it is carried forward indefinitely (quarantined) and applied to future capital gains.
A disposal (sale) of an asset that triggers CGT is called a CGT event. Division 104-5 identifies 56 CGT events or ways to dispose of such assets. However, two events occur in 95% of cases:

A1: Disposal of a CGT Asset
These include the change of legal ownership (sale, transfer, exchange, gift) or destruction of such assets, where timing is usually determined by the date when the contract is signed or the date of settlement in the absence of a contract.
C1: Loss or Destruction of a CGT Asset
Here, the timing will depend on whether the taxpayer receives compensation in respect to this event.

If the CGT asset is insured, a CGT event occurs when the taxpayer first receives compensation/insurance payment.
If the CGT asset is not insured, C1 occurs when the destruction or loss happens or is first discovered. Note: capital losses are calculated as cost base minus capital proceeds, where cost base is at historical cost (not the market value at the time of destruction).

title: CGT Calculator
text:
The 2026 Reform
The Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Act 2026 received Royal Assent on 26 June 2026. Its main CGT changes apply from 1 July 2027. Until then, the existing discount rules continue to apply.

title: CGT Calculator
text:
Existing CGT discount rules

Under the rules applying before 1 July 2027, if a CGT asset is held for 12 months or more, the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) allows elligible individuals and trusts to discount to 50% the capital gain (proceeds minus cost base) after offsetting any carried forward capital losses.
A complying superannuation fund may generally apply a 33⅓% discount.
Companies are not eligible for the CGT discount.
Other conditions, including residency and asset type, can affect eligibility.

title: CGT Calculator
text:
Changes from 1 July 2027

From 1 July 2027, the general 50% discount is replaced by cost-base indexation for relevant gains of individuals, trusts and partnerships.
A 30% minimum tax may also apply to relevant capital gains of Australian-resident individuals, including gains flowing through certain trusts and partnerships. Indexation adjusts eligible cost-base elements for inflation; the third element, which includes certain ownership costs, is excluded.


Exception for qualifying new dwellings and affordable housing

For a CGT event on or after 1 July 2027 relating to a qualifying new residential dwelling, the 50% discount remains available. The existing discount for qualifying affordable housing, which can be up to 60%, is also preserved. Investors in qualifying new builds may choose either the 50% discount or the new indexation and minimum-tax treatment, subject to the statutory eligibility rules.
The discount is therefore not removed from all existing property gains: gains accrued before 1 July 2027 retain their pre-reform treatment under transitional rules. Assets held across that date may be subject to special cost-base and apportionment rules.

Official sources: Treasury Laws Amendment (Tax Reform No. 1) Act 2026 · Treasury summary of the 2026–27 Budget tax changes

title: Fringe Benefits Tax
text:
What is Fringe Benefit Tax (FBT)?

Fringe Benefit Tax (FBT) is levied on any non-cash benefit that employers (or employers’ associates/subsidiaries) provide to employees (or employees’ associates) used for private purposes.

Employees for FBT purposes include: company directors, officeholders, employees, and recipients of compensation payments
Associates of employees are: their relatives (S318 ITAA36) + any other person (friend, flatmate…).

FBT exclusions

Payments of: salary/wages, cash allowances (except a living-away-from-home allowance), superannuation, benefits under Div83A scheme, ETP and specific exemptions under FBTAA (1986)
Payments to non-employees: genuine contractors, clients, shareholders and suppliers

Common fringe benefits include: company car, home electricity/home telephone bills, private health insurance, children’s school fees, private holiday, low or interest-free loans, entertainment (meals, free concert ticket…)
Benefits are grouped into the 12 categories

Car fringe *
Debt waiver fringe
Loan fringe *
Expense payment fringe *
Housing fringe
Living-away-from-home allowance fringe
Board fringe
Meal entertainment fringe
Tax-exempt body entertainment fringe
Property fringe *
Car parking fringe
Residual fringe (i.e. benefits that do not fall under any of the other eleven categories)

title: Fringe Benefits Tax
text:
FBT Administration

The FBT regime runs from 1 April to 31 March
FBT is a self-assessed return prepared by the employer, and is a separate form from BAS and IAS
If self-prepared, FBT must be lodged and paid by 21 May, or 25 June if lodged by a tax agent
If the taxpayer’s FBT is less than $3,000, the liability is settled in one annual payment by one of the above due dates.
If more than the threshold, the ATO requires FBT to be paid in quarterly instalments plus an annual payment of any outstanding amount, in which case Label F1 of the taxpayer’s BAS will be shown.
F1 is the annual FBT estimate provided by the ATO based on the taxpayer’s prior FBT assessment, and it is pre-printed on the Activity Statement. Taxpayers can vary (adjust) their quarterly instalments based on their updated estimate for the FBT year ending 31 March. The ATO provides several reasons for making these variations.
FBT rate typically corresponds to the highest marginal tax rate plus Medicare levy. A 47% rate currently applies across the 31 March 2022 to 31 March 2026 FBT years.
Section 136(1) of the Act broadly defines a benefit to include “any right, privilege, service or facility”, which encompasses anything of value provided as part of or in lieu of a salary package (except for salary and wages), which is designed to reduce the income tax liability of the employee.
The taxable value of a fringe benefit must be grossed up before calculating the fringe benefit tax. Grossing up helps to equate non-cash benefits with salary levels, enabling the ATO to tax these benefits as if they were income. This process allows for a fair comparison between different types of compensation.
The gross-up factor depends on whether the employer can claim GST credit related to the cost of providing the benefit. Type 1 fringes are GST credit claimable, whereas Type 2 fringes are those that are not Type 1 benefits (i.e., either the benefit is GST-free or the employer is not eligible to claim an input tax).


Further details and official requirements are published on the ATO’s website.
